description: We are a team of four students from diverse engineering backgrounds who love solving complex problems with an entrepreneurial mindset. We see this edition of NASA Space Apps hackathon as the foundational milestone for our future startup!
summary: "Ceres" is a cloud-native platform for data analysis, visualisation & algorithmic predictions, sourcing data from open-source NASA APIs, governments' local cadastral data, as well as bespoke custom ground probes hardware, in order to generate different crop rotation plans, optimising for the farmer's individual needs.
details:
Project "Ceres" converts raw orbital Earth observations, legal land boundaries, and local IoT device sensor telemetry into actionable 3-year crop rotation plans.

The full GitHub repository is available and open-source, dual-licensed as MIT/Apache-2.0.

Main points

  • Parcel & Land-Cover Filtering: Farmers select exact fields via government cadastral polygons (Agenzia delle Entrate INSPIRE WFS) or OpenStreetMap Overpass, filtered with ESA WorldCover (10 m) to isolate active cropland and pastures.
    • Field-Scale (30–70 m): NASA HLS v2.0 (NDVI, NDMI, NDRE, low-vigor fraction, 5-year crop history), NASA ECOSTRESS v2 (70 m daily ET, ESI, surface temp), NASA NASADEM (elevation, slope, >8° erosion share, waterlogging risk).
    • Regional & Climate (250 m–300 km): NASA SMAP L4 (9 km surface & root-zone soil moisture), GPM IMERG V07 (precipitation & dry days), NASA POWER (agroclimatology, GDD, 1991–2020 normals), MODIS MOD16A2 v6.1 (ET backup), GRACE-FO (groundwater trends), NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 (2030s/2050s SSP2-4.5/SSP5-8.5 drought risk), ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 (texture, SOC, pH, N, CEC, bulk density), plus 14 NASA GIBS WMTS layers.
  • Ground-Truth Hardware: A low-cost ESP32-S3 probe in a custom 3D-printed enclosure streams in-situ soil moisture, humidity, and temperature per plot to calibrate local baselines.
  • Deterministic Optimization: Evaluates 3-year sequences across a 12-crop catalog using peer-reviewed models (whitepaper on GitHub, link is further below): FAO-56 Penman-Monteith/Hargreaves ET0 & USDA-SCS water balance, RUSLE erosion, Herridge N-fixation, IPCC 2019 N2O/leaching, Hénin-Dupuis SOC, ASAE cone-index compaction (ΔPSI), and Eurostat/EC/FAOSTAT/World Bank economics. Outputs 5 pathways (Most Income, Highest ROI, Best Soil Health, Least Effort, Least Risk) plus a "Where Satellite Data Needs Local Eyes" checklist.

Scientific Validity & Mathematical Models

Every yield, water, soil, and financial metric is computed deterministically before any natural-language formatting occurs.

The algorithm's whitepaper is available on our GitHub repository.
A brief summary of the methods:

  • Crop Water Balance (FAO-56 & USDA-SCS): Combines crop-specific evapotranspiration coefficients (Kc), reference evapotranspiration (ET0 via FAO-56 Penman-Monteith / Hargreaves-Samani from NASA POWER & ECOSTRESS), USDA-SCS effective rainfall (GPM IMERG), and Saxton-Rawls / SMAP root-zone moisture storage to calculate seasonal irrigation deficits (m³/ha).
  • Topsoil Erosion (RUSLE): Estimates annual soil loss (A = R × K × LS × C × P) under both current vegetation cover and bare-soil intervals using NASA POWER 1991–2020 / GloREDa rainfall erosivity, SoilGrids texture/organic matter erodibility (Williams/EPIC), NASADEM slope length/steepness, and HLS NDVI cover factors.
  • Nitrogen, Carbon & Compaction Dynamics: Tracks biological nitrogen fixation (Herridge), IPCC 2019 N2O/leaching and synthetic fertilizer requirements, Hénin-Dupuis soil organic carbon (SOC) trajectories, and ASAE cone-index subsoil compaction (ΔPSI) vs. taproot biodrilling across multi-year machinery passes.
  • Economic & Market Calibration: Integrates Eurostat & EC Agrifood farm-gate crop prices, EC Weekly Oil Bulletin diesel tariffs, FAOSTAT national yields, and World Bank Pink Sheet fertilizer/commodity trends, while allowing farm administrators to override values with their own utility rates or lab soil tests.

Tools, Tech Stack & Production Infrastructure

Ceres was built from scratch during the hackathon as a containerized, multi-service cloud-native platform:

  • Frontend (web): Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui with custom styles and components) with interactive Leaflet mapping (Esri World Imagery, OpenStreetMap, AdE Catasto WMS, and NASA GIBS overlays).
  • Backend & Aggregation (web-api, data-api, analytics-api): Three asynchronous FastAPI microservices handling parallel NASA Earthdata/CMR/STAC retrieval, spatial clipping, Fmask cloud masking, unit normalization, and deterministic rotation optimization.
  • Database, Auth & Role-Based Access: PocketBase (SQLite) managing user authentication, farm organizations, cached satellite snapshots, IoT telemetry, and role-based permissions.
  • Hardware & Firmware: ESP32-S3 microcontroller with capacitive soil moisture and temperature/humidity sensing, custom firmware for periodic telemetry ingestion, and a custom CAD-designed enclosure.
  • Production Deployment: Containerized with Docker and Docker Compose, deployed on a Hetzner Cloud VPS in Helsinki, Finland behind Caddy HTTPS reverse-proxying (nasa.zeph.work) from a Cloudflare-managed DNS server, with persistent volume storage and multi-tier memory/SQLite caching for sub-second dashboard loads without overloading upstream NASA servers.

Key Design Factors Considered

  • Farmer-First Information Architecture: Most Earth-observation tools overwhelm non-scientists with raw spectral bands and jargon. We organized the plot workspace around farmer decisions (Field & Map, Water, Soil & Climate, Rotation Plan, Markets & Costs), leading with a concise editorial briefing while keeping full scientific tables and formula citations one click away.
    • This does not mean scientists are out of the picture: Ceres does its best to present the data at different levels of abstraction, but everything remains accessible to experts.
    • Future plans include exporting the data in standardized formats, in order to ease scientists' work involving it.
  • Explicit Scale & Uncertainty Transparency: Every metric clearly distinguishes parcel-level measurements (30 m–70 m) from regional context (250 m–300 km). Where satellite resolution cannot detect localized conditions—such as subsoil hardpan or tile drainage—Ceres automatically generates a "Where Satellite Data Needs Local Eyes" inspection checklist rather than overstating orbital precision.
  • Low-CAPEX Adoption Path: Agricultural margins leave little room for expensive proprietary stations. By keeping the software fully functional using open satellite and cadastral data alone while designing the ESP32 probe to be as low-cost as possible, farms can onboard with zero upfront hardware risk and deploy ground nodes selectively where microclimate precision matters most.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • For Small and Mid-Sized Farmers: Eliminates guesswork in multi-year crop planning, cutting unnecessary irrigation and synthetic nitrogen inputs while protecting soil organic matter and preventing compaction-driven yield loss.
  • For Agronomists & Cooperatives: Enables multi-parcel monitoring across fragmented landholdings with auditable physical calculations, exportable telemetry, and shared read-only farm workspaces.
  • Broader Scalability: Because the core data pipeline relies on global NASA Earth observations and open standards, Ceres can scale seamlessly from fragmented European cadastral parcels to smallholder and commercial farms worldwide.
Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure: Google Gemini is integrated into Project Ceres strictly as a plain-language translation layer for pre-computed deterministic algorithm outputs, and was also used during development to assist with prototyping, scaffolding, refactoring, code review, documentation formatting, and fact-checking. This document was written with SI assistance, alongside manual corrections and formatting.
